title: Ha'azinu: give ear, O heavens (Deuteronomy 32:1)
hookLine: Moses' last song calls heaven and earth as witnesses

cards: Open a Torah scroll almost anywhere and you see columns of text running edge to edge, like the pages of a book. Then you reach Ha'azinu, and the page changes shape.

The words split into two narrow columns with a gap down the middle, line answering line. Scribes still copy it that way today. Even someone who can't read Hebrew can see that something different is happening.
These words of Moses aren't a speech. They're a song.

teach.b: It begins: "Give ear, ye heavens, and I will speak; And let the earth hear the words of my mouth." Ha'azinu means give ear: listen closely. In Nitzavim, Moses had called heaven and earth as witnesses.
Now he speaks to them directly. Why the sky and the ground? Rashi gives two reasons.
First, they last. Moses is mortal, and so is everyone listening, but heaven and earth will still be there to testify long after. Second, they respond.
If the people keep the covenant, the heavens give rain and the earth gives its crops; if not, they hold back.
There's a playful midrash in the Sifrei too.
Moses says give ear to the heavens, the word for listening up close, and only hear to the earth, the word for listening from further off, because he was near to heaven and far from earth.

teach.h: ISAIAH SAYS IT THE OTHER WAY.
teach.b: The prophet Isaiah, the midrash notes, says it the other way round: hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth.
He was nearer the earth. Under the play is a real point: where you stand shapes how you speak. The song itself is long and fierce, a retelling of the people's story, its gifts and its failures.
It's read in synagogue in the fall, around the High Holy Days. And it opens by calling the whole world to listen: the sky above, the ground below, and everyone in between.

how: Ha'azinu is read in synagogue in the fall, usually on the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur or just after; in the Torah scroll it is written in a special two-column layout.

o: give ear: the first word of Moses' song
go forth: Moses sending the people on
rejoice: the song sung at the festival

games.q: inside the song's first line — tap the pairs.
p: hear, O heavens; give ear, O earth

s: Ha'azinu is written in the scroll like ordinary prose
scribes lay it out in two columns.
Rashi says heaven and earth are witnesses partly because they endure
they'll outlast Moses and everyone listening.

games.q: you're Moses, about to die, and you need witnesses who will outlast everyone in the camp. who do you call?
games.why: 'give ear, ye heavens... let the earth hear': witnesses that last, and that answer with rain and crops.

practice: If you can, go to a window or step outside; if not, picture it. Look up at the sky, cloud or blue or dark, then down at the ground, grass or pavement or floor, the two Moses called to listen because they last.
Let yourself be small between them for a breath.

wordCard.voice: Ha'azinu. Give ear. The first word of Moses' last song, spoken to the sky.

orig.note: Hebrew: give ear, listen. the first word of Deuteronomy 32 and the name of the portion.

carryVoice: Your line: heaven and earth listen. Still there long after everyone listening is gone. Day five hundred twenty-seven, done.

sources.q: Give ear, ye heavens, and I will speak; And let the earth hear the words of my mouth.
